channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: The Labor Department reports US import prices rose 1.1% in September and 8.1% from a year earlier, the largest 12-month gain since July 2022, with imported fuel up 4.8% on the month, MarketScreener reports.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports that, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, US import prices rose 1.1% in September after a downwardly revised 0.5% rise in August, and by 8.1% in the 12 months to September, the largest annual gain since July 2022, after 6.7% in August. Imported fuel prices rebounded 4.8% in September after falling 0.2% in August. The row attributes the monthly rise to higher costs for energy products and a range of other goods, and describes it as further evidence of rising inflation pressure as the Middle East conflict continues. It adds that economists have attributed rising inflation to President Trump's policies, including tariffs on imports, and the Middle East conflict. The row does not split the index between fuel and other goods for the annual figure, or give figures by country of origin or product group such as chemicals.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the index measures prices of goods entering the US, which may differ from what US buyers paid after tariffs, and a rise of this size feeds into the cost of imported materials and into the inflation data that central banks weigh, and the fuel component shows the energy effect. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher import prices could raise the cost of raw materials sourced abroad for US production and tighten margins where costs cannot be passed on. Points that may be worth considering include the October release, the Federal Reserve's next rate decision, and the split between fuel and other goods.

MarketScreener

item.title: China's National Bureau of Statistics reports third-quarter GDP growth of 4.5% from a year earlier, up from 4.3% in the second quarter, and 4.6% for January to September, within the 4.5% to 5.0% annual target, Channel News Asia reports.
item.description:
Channel News Asia reports that China's National Bureau of Statistics said on 19 October that GDP grew 4.5% year on year in the third quarter, above expectations, after 4.3% in the second quarter, which it calls a more-than-three-year low; the economy grew 4.6% in the first nine months, within the government's annual target of 4.5% to 5.0%. On a quarterly basis GDP rose 1.2%, against 0.9% in the second quarter and an expected 1.1%. A Reuters poll cited by MarketScreener had expected 4.4% year on year. BBC gives growth of 5% for January to March. China Economic Net gives nine-month GDP of CNY 107.11 trillion, with primary industry up 3.7%, secondary industry up 3.8% and tertiary industry up 5.2%. Channel News Asia adds that in September China's trade surplus widened more than expected as exports surged, putting it on track to exceed last year's record of USD 1.2 trillion and likely to intensify trade tensions with major partners. The rows give no breakdown by spending, investment or property.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The figures are national accounts, with an export-led September. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, growth within the target range lowers the pressure for further stimulus, while a widening trade surplus adds to trade friction with partners that run deficits with China. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, China's growth and exports shape demand for bonding, sealing and coating products at manufacturers there and the competitive pressure on producers elsewhere, and trade-defence responses could change input costs. Points that may be worth considering include fourth-quarter data, property and consumption indicators, and the response of trading partners to the surplus.

Channel News Asia | BBC | China Economic Net | MarketScreener

item.title: The Fed reports US industrial production rose 0.7% in September, the sixth consecutive monthly rise, with manufacturing output up 0.3%; the New York Fed's October index rose to 25.5 while the Philadelphia Fed's fell to 20.9.
item.description:
Yahoo Taiwan reports that, according to the Federal Reserve, US industrial production rose 0.7% from the previous month in September 2026, the sixth consecutive monthly rise and above the 0.5% the market expected, and that manufacturing output rebounded by 0.3%, in line with expectations. Its headline says the annual gain was the largest in four years, but the summary gives no annual figure. The row adds that supply chain disruptions linked to the Middle East conflict, rising energy prices and higher borrowing costs continue to weigh on the outlook. Dünya reports that the New York Fed's manufacturing index rose by 17.9 points to 25.5 in October from 7.6 in September, with the new orders index up 21.2 points to 23.2, the shipments index up 16.3 points to 13.1 and the index of future business conditions down 8 points to 21; the Philadelphia Fed's index fell from 37.8 in September to 20.9 in October. The two regional surveys cover different regions and are not combined with the national production figure. The rows give no breakdown by industry, no figure for chemicals or materials output, and no explanation for the opposite regional moves.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The production data are measured outputs, while the regional indexes are survey readings that point in different directions. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, six months of rising industrial production suggest industrial activity has held up despite higher energy and borrowing costs, although manufacturing output only rebounded by 0.3% in September, and the opposite regional survey moves suggest the pace is uneven. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, US manufacturing output underlies demand for industrial bonding, sealing and coating products, and an uneven recovery could mean uneven orders across customer industries. Points that may be worth considering include the October production release, the next regional surveys, and the Federal Reserve's next rate decision.

Yahoo Taiwan | Dünya Gazetesi

item.title: A Putin decree places Russian assets of Tarkett, Menshen and other Western firms under temporary administration, Handelsblatt and the Moscow Times report; Handelsblatt says the Kremlin calls it reversible and a reaction to EU states' role in the war.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that a decree by President Putin places the local assets of several European companies under temporary state administration, naming Menshen, which it describes as a German packaging manufacturer, Tarkett, a French flooring manufacturer, Sverige International Holdings, a Swedish packaging producer, and Sonoco, which it calls a Dutch packaging manufacturer. The Kremlin states that the measure is a reaction to the role of EU states in the war and adds that the decision is reversible. The Moscow Times reports that the Russian assets of five manufacturers are placed under the temporary management of Tsentr Kapital Management Company: Tarkett, the hygiene manufacturer Ontex Ru, Menshen, the corrugated producer Kappa Rus and the metal packaging producer Eviosys, which it describes as a subsidiary of the US Sonoco Products. It gives their combined 2025 revenue as more than RUB 53 billion, with Tarkett at RUB 19.3 billion, Kappa Rus at RUB 16.5 billion, Ontex Ru at RUB 10.3 billion, Eviosys at RUB 6.1 billion and Menshen at RUB 1.4 billion. The two outlets list different companies and give different parent nationalities for Sonoco. The rows do not give the legal basis, how long the administration lasts, what happens to the owners' rights, or the conditions for reversal.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a decree on named companies, with combined 2025 revenue of more than RUB 53 billion according to the Moscow Times. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a reversible administration order used as a reaction to EU policy signals that Western assets in Russia can be targeted in response to what the Kremlin describes as the role of EU states in the war, and the list includes producers in packaging and flooring. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, packaging and flooring producers are customers for bonding and coating products, and measures against their Russian subsidiaries affect those customers' operations there rather than demand in other markets. Points that may be worth considering include whether more companies are added, the conditions for reversal, and any EU response.

Handelsblatt | Moscow Times

item.title: The Straits Times reports EU leaders approved on 16 October the Beijing deal to cut Chinese electric vehicle exports and authorised the Commission to create trade defence tools without delay, with proposals expected by end-2026.
item.description:
The Straits Times reports that on 16 October 2026 EU leaders approved a trade deal concluded in Beijing earlier in October, under which China voluntarily agreed to cut by almost half its exports of electric vehicles to Europe, but that member states judged the concession insufficient for bigger trade questions and authorised the Commission to create "without delay" a toolbox of new trade defence instruments, including a "killer switch" provision allowing quotas and tariffs at a moment's notice; the Commission is expected to come forward with proposals by the end of 2026. China Economic Net describes a consensus on hybrid vehicle trade that uses the 2025 trade volume as a baseline and allows room for growth, while the Straits Times describes a cut of almost half in electric vehicle exports; the rows give no baseline for "almost half" and do not say whether the two describe the same arrangement. Chinatimes says the second meeting of the China–EU trade and investment consultation mechanism reached 16 consensuses in four areas, trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property and WTO reform. Cnyes reports that senior economic officials meeting in Bangkok formally established a new agreement mechanism aimed at addressing economic imbalances; its headline calls it a high-level working group on "orderly rebalancing". The South China Morning Post says China's commerce ministry warned the EU not to "fantasise" that a hard line would force concessions, and that the EU confirmed plans for a new kill switch. Commercial Times reports that Commission President von der Leyen listed chemicals and industrial machinery as priority industries for protection at the 15 October summit. The rows do not say which sectors the toolbox would cover or which instruments beyond quotas and tariffs it would include; Lianhe Zaobao says the next round of talks between the EU and China will be held in March 2027. The rows give 15 October for the summit and 16 October for the approval and do not reconcile the two.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a mandate to prepare instruments, not instruments in force. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a tool that can impose quotas or tariffs at short notice makes import conditions less predictable for sectors it covers, and it could provoke responses from China on exports of materials and components. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, a toolbox that reached chemicals could change the cost and availability of materials sourced from China, while any Chinese response on export controls could affect inputs and equipment. Points that may be worth considering include the Commission's proposals at the end of 2026, which products they name, and China's reaction.

Straits Times | China Economic Net | Chinatimes | Cnyes | South China Morning Post | Commercial Times | Lianhe Zaobao

item.title: KPMG's survey finds 86% of German CEOs expect growth over the next three years, up 14 percentage points, and nearly 70% expect profit growth of 2.5% or more, Süddeutsche Zeitung reports.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung reports that German CEOs look more optimistically at their companies' prospects for the first time in years, according to a survey by the auditing and consulting firm KPMG: 86% expect growth in the next three years, up 14 percentage points from the previous year, and nearly 70% expect profit growth of 2.5% or more for their company over the next three years. It gives the share of optimists as 77% in 2024 and 80% in 2023. Handelsblatt gives the same 86% and 14-point rise. A rise of 14 points to 86% implies 72% a year earlier, which matches neither reported share, and the rows do not say what the 14 points compare with. Handelsblatt adds that more economists are confident the German economy will grow faster in 2026, and that the German government more than doubled its 2026 forecast to 1.3%. The rows do not give the number of CEOs surveyed, their sectors, the survey dates, and do not say how the survey defines growth.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report expectations of executives, not orders or output. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, optimism among CEOs can precede investment and hiring, but it can also change quickly when energy prices and interest rates move. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German customers' investment plans affect demand for bonding, sealing and coating products in manufacturing and construction, and the survey gives no sector breakdown to say where. Points that may be worth considering include whether Ifo and other German business indicators show the same change, German orders data, and the next government forecast.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Handelsblatt

item.title: China Economic Net reports that industrial value added rose 5.5% in September, with the product list showing cement down 5.3%, steel down 3.8%, automobiles down 5.7% and ethylene up 6.4%; the row gives no period for the product figures.
item.description:
China Economic Net reports, in a row published on 19 October, that value added of industrial enterprises above designated size rose 5.5% year on year in September, 0.3 percentage points faster than in August, and 5.3% in the first nine months; mining rose 1.3%, manufacturing 6.0% and electricity, heat, gas and water supply 5.6%. Of 626 products, 271 showed year-on-year output growth. The product list gives steel at 118.17 million tonnes (down 3.8%), cement at 144.01 million tonnes (down 5.3%), ten non-ferrous metals at 6.93 million tonnes (up 0.1%), ethylene at 3.55 million tonnes (up 6.4%) and automobiles at 3.063 million units (down 5.7%). The row does not say whether these are September or cumulative figures. A second row from the same outlet reports that China's construction business activity index rose 3.4 percentage points from August to 50.3% in September, the cement shipment rate rose 2.2 percentage points to 40.5%, and new special-purpose bond issuance rose by CNY 101.5 billion from August to CNY 620.4 billion. The row attributes the index to the National Bureau of Statistics and names no source for the cement shipment and bond figures. The rows give no regional split and no figures for chemicals other than ethylene.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The product list mixes construction materials, metals, a chemical and vehicles, and gives no period. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, falling cement output points to weaker demand for construction materials, rising ethylene output points to more petrochemical supply, and lower vehicle output lowers demand for materials used in assembly; a construction index above 50 is conventionally read as expansion on that measure. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, China's construction and vehicle volumes bear on demand for bonding, sealing and coating products, while higher ethylene output affects feedstock supply in the region. Points that may be worth considering include whether the period of the product figures is confirmed, the next monthly releases, and property and vehicle data.

China Economic Net, industrial output | China Economic Net, construction index

item.title: Trump waived certain Graham Act sanctions and duties on Russia, including tariffs on buyers of Russian oil and gas, before the 18 October start; Rubio says the President will take up to 60 days to assess the impact, and Brent futures fell to USD 108.43.
item.description:
The Economic Times reports that an executive order invokes Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to waive certain sanctions, restrictions and the duties under Sections 112 and 113, which concern tariffs on Russian goods and on goods from countries linked to Russian oil and gas purchases or sanctions evasion, while the President keeps the authority to reinstate them. BBC says the law was signed in September and was due to take effect on 18 October; HuffPost says it provides for tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas. Business Standard reports that the waivers stay in effect until the President or the Secretary of State determines further action is appropriate; it adds that Trump wants a 60-day period to analyse what sanctions on Russia and tariffs on other countries would mean for the global economy, and the Economic Times oil-price report quotes Rubio saying the President will take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact. The Straits Times reports that the administration cast the waiver as a way to facilitate a diesel deal with Russia. On 19 October Brent crude futures fell to USD 108.43 a barrel, down from a peak of USD 110, the Economic Times reports, adding that the waiver may lead to more Russian fuel supplies; the row gives no date for the peak and no closing price. The Economic Times reports that the waiver of the proposed tariffs of up to 100% has eased uncertainty for Indian exporters ahead of the pre-Christmas shipping season but is unlikely to reverse their move to reduce dependence on the US market, and the think tank GTRI calls it temporary relief that could be withdrawn at any time. Arab News reports that lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order, and the Straits Times reports that Republican members of Congress criticised it and that Senator Ted Cruz said the administration should have found other ways to lower fuel costs; Zelenskyy said a loosening of pressure on Russia and financial rewards would only encourage Putin to continue striking. The rows differ on the order's date, 16 or 17 October, and Anadolu's headline says Trump imposed a 500% duty while its own summary says the tariffs were waived; no other cited row mentions a 500% duty.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a temporary waiver that can be reversed, not a repeal. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the waiver removes for now a tariff threat on large buyers of Russian oil and gas and could add Russian fuel to markets short of diesel, which could ease energy and freight costs, while a reinstatement would bring back both the threat and the uncertainty. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, energy and petrochemical feedstock costs feed into raw material prices, so a lasting easing in oil prices could lower input costs over time, while tariff uncertainty for buyers such as India affects trade flows in chemicals and materials. The rows give no volume for the Russian fuel that could reach markets. Points that may be worth considering include the end of the 60-day assessment, any response from Congress, and the oil price after the waiver.

Economic Times, executive order | BBC | HuffPost | Business Standard | Straits Times | Economic Times, oil prices | Economic Times, Indian exporters | Economic Times, GTRI | Arab News | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Anadolu Agency

item.title: Handelsblatt, citing the Federal Statistical Office, reports German permits for 169,400 apartments in January to August, up a good 12%, while Wirtschafts Woche reports Ifo's residential construction climate fell to minus 25.1 in September from minus 22.5.
item.description:
Handelsblatt, citing the Federal Statistical Office, reports that German authorities issued permits for 169,400 apartments in new and existing buildings from January to August 2026, a rise of a good 12%, or 18,300, on the same period of 2025; 137,500 were in new buildings, up 12.7%. In August alone permits covered 20,600 apartments, up 6.8%, or 1,300, from a year earlier, after a rise of a good 15% in the first half, the strongest first-half increase since 2016. Permits for multi-family buildings covered 90,600 apartments, up 14.5%, permits for single-family houses rose by nearly 8% and those for two-family houses by 21.7%. Tagesschau gives 12.1% for new apartments in the first eight months, while Handelsblatt gives a good 12% for apartments in new and existing buildings and 12.7% for new buildings; 18,300 on a base of 151,100 is 12.1%, but the rows do not reconcile the labels. Handelsblatt adds that the building minister announced a federally owned housing company, with the goal that it starts in 2027. Wirtschafts Woche reports that the Ifo business climate barometer for German residential construction fell to minus 25.1 in September from minus 22.5 in August, that 41.3% of companies reported a lack of orders, unchanged, and that 14.1% reported cancelled orders, up from 13.4%; it says rising energy prices due to the Middle East war prompted the ECB to raise its key rate from 2.25% to 2.50% in September, that construction interest rates have risen, making project financing more expensive, and that many economists expect another rise in December. Permits count approvals; the rows give no figures for construction starts or completions.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows combine approval counts with a survey-based climate index; neither measures construction output. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, permits tend to lead starts and completions by months, so rising approvals can precede more building, while missing orders, cancellations and higher financing costs can delay projects that already hold permits. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, residential building uses bonding, sealing and coating products in insulation, flooring and facades, so permitted projects that start would raise demand with a lag, and the Ifo reading suggests firms do not yet see that. Points that may be worth considering include whether approvals turn into starts, how Ifo's order and cancellation shares develop, and the ECB's December decision.

Handelsblatt | Tagesschau | Wirtschafts Woche

item.title: Euronews reports that the Franco-German car deal would require 70% European production of components excluding batteries and 10% European battery content, with a 90% fleet CO2 cut by 2035; Die Zeit says it is not yet a decision.
item.description:
Euronews reports that on 16 October 2026 France and Germany reached a deal under which 70% of car components, excluding batteries, would have to be produced in Europe and 10% of battery content would have to come from European sources, and carmakers would have to cut fleet-average CO2 emissions by 90% by 2035 without offsetting the remaining 10%, contrary to the Commission's initial proposal. La Repubblica says the agreement was formalised in a joint declaration after the Macron–Merz meeting and that the remaining 10% is linked to renewable fuels in the circulating fleet. The South China Morning Post says "Made in Europe" would cover only the 27 EU member states, with an opt-in for European partners that were in the single market on 1 January 2020, and that cars would also need to meet a research and development requirement to qualify for public procurement or subsidies. Yahoo reports that the UK could qualify only if it adopted EU trade protection measures, including tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, and that Japan, South Korea and Turkey would stay outside. An NZZ opinion piece says purchase premiums would go only to electric cars made in the EU and EFTA states; the rows differ on how far "Made in Europe" extends beyond the 27 member states and do not reconcile this. Die Zeit says the paper is not a decision of the EU or of the two governments, because their environment ministers consider the 90% CO2 passage wrong, and Yahoo France says final approval from Germany's SPD was still awaited. VDA President Hildegard Müller calls the agreement an important step that in relevant points still falls short of the necessary adjustments, and says further discussion and adjustment are needed in the Council and Parliament; IG Metall welcomes it. The rows do not say how a component's European share is measured or when the Council and Parliament vote.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a joint position of France and Germany, which Die Zeit says is not a decision of the two governments, on proposals that still need the Council and the Parliament, so no rule is in force. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, content thresholds of 70% for components and 10% for batteries, if applied to qualification for subsidies and public contracts as the South China Morning Post describes for "Made in Europe", would change which suppliers and sites qualify for sales that depend on public money, while a 90% CO2 target lets carmakers keep selling combustion models for longer. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicles built in Europe from European components could raise demand from suppliers with EU sites, and longer production of combustion models could keep demand for bonding, sealing and coating products used in both drive-train types; an opt-in for European partners, which Yahoo says the UK could use only if it adopted EU trade protection measures, would widen the qualifying area. The rows do not say how origin would be counted. Points that may be worth considering include the Council and Parliament positions, how origin is measured, and whether the UK adopts the conditions attached to its opt-in.

Euronews | La Repubblica | South China Morning Post | Yahoo | Neue Zürcher Zeitung | Die Zeit | Yahoo France | VDA | IG Metall
